    Promoting clean hand practice among street food vendors

    Understanding human behaviour

    The goal of behavioral design is to understand how people think, feel, and act in order to create designs that influence their behavior in a positive way.

    Project timeline :

    4 weeks

    Team :

    Swetha l Disha l Pramoddini

    Aim

    Objectives

    Scope

    To identify and implement behavior change in the context of street food

    To observe human behavior in the context of street food

    To identify target behavior

    To implement behavioral change

    The study focuses on street food in Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar, India. It looks at street food from the behavioral lens.

    Street food: An introduction

    Street meals are ready-to-eat foods and beverages produced and/or sold by vendors or hawkers in public areas such as streets and other public areas.

    ​

    ​

    Street foods have a long history in many nations throughout the world, and they are resourceful as well as imaginative. The cuisine is influenced by local and traditional cultures. Around 2.5 billion people worldwide consume street food. Many cities around the world are known for their street food, and it had become a crucial part of their identities.

    Source : Netflix

    Research Methodology

    The research was divided into 3 phases:

     

    Phase 1: Research and Observations

    Various street food markets and stalls were visited multiple times, to be able to identify common patterns among the different typologies of street food stalls.

    ​

    Phase 2: Identifying target behavior

    Deviant behaviors were identified from the previous phase, and a target behavior was chosen, which had to be converted to the desired behavior.

     

    Phase 3: Attempting to change target behavior

    The drivers behind the behavior were understood and targeted to bring in change, various ideation techniques were employed to bring in a  concept that can be taken ahead and tested out, and improvements were made based on the feedback received.

    Delving deeper into Hygiene in street food

    Street food vending has become an important public health issue and a great concern to everybody. This is due to widespread food borne diseases. Major sources contributing to microbial contamination are the place of preparation, utensils for cooking and serving, raw materials, time and temperature abuse of cooked foods and the personal hygiene of vendors.

    - Street Vended Food in Developing World: Hazard Analyses by Sharmila Rane, 2011

    PERSONAL HYGIENE

    • The vendors do not have adequate washing facilities, and some vendors started their duties without taking a proper bath.
       

      Some food handlers washed their hands in the same bucket used for cleaning utensils, which may lead to the contamination of food with faecal matter.


      According to the Public Health Association, only 53% of Indians wash their hands with soap after defecating; 38% do so before eating and only 30% before preparing food

    What can be done to counter it?

    Clean utensils

    Clean clothes

    Clean hands

    MICROBIOLOGICAL HYGIENE

    • Improper cooking and handling of food may result in the presence of foodborne bacterial agents

      ​

    What can be done to counter it?

    Washing hands with soap

    Proper storage of raw materials

    Use of clean water

    CHEMICAL CONTAMINATION

    • Nonfood grade chemical additives, such as colorants and preservatives, and contaminants

    ​

    • Concern that food may be contaminated with heavy metals and pesticide residues. These contaminants may come from the utensils, raw materials, or transport methods used and may also occur due to the lack of appropriate storage facilities.

    What can be done to counter it?

    Better Quality Ingredients

    Better Quality utensils

    Check on chemical contamination

    ENVIRONMENTAL HYGIENE

    • Inadequate refuse disposal facilities lead to the accumulation of refuse at food vending sites. This leads to an increased pest population and resulted in an increased risk of food contamination.

    Covered Food items 

    Proper waste disposal

    What can be done to counter it?

    Clean surroundings

    Why isn't street food perceived to be hygienic?

    Understanding why does poor hygiene persists in street food, and how it leads to the enforcement of informality.

    Target behavior

    Street food vendors lack personal hygiene practices which adds to the misuse of informality in street food sector

    Desired behaviour

    Vendors should show visible personal hygiene at their thelas. . . .

    To understand the factors of visible personal hygiene

    By magnifying the lenses of the problem, a specific behaviour problem was identified which falls under the lens of informality.

    Final desired behaviour

    Vendors should show visible hygiene at their thelas by using a separate cloth to wipe their hands when making or serving food to customers.

    Why vendors?

    The vendor is the only constant participant in the street food thela space while the customers keep changing.

     

    A vendor can take ownership and dictate this space to create expectations and boundaries for people moving in that space.

    Why chaat thelas?

    Chaat thelas are where uncooked or semi cooked food is served. Hands are used a lot in the process and most vendors use bare hands.

    Customers also stand around the thela, getting a clear view of the vendor preparing their food.

    Motivations to clean their hands

    BCD study by Aunger & Curtis suggests identification of key drivers to influence behaviour change. Some of the potential drivers identified are:

    Framework of behavior change model

    • In order to tackle the misuse of informality in his space, he should be emotionally equipped for it. The confidence and proficiency in his profession improves with the reassurance that he serves clean, good, quality food. The extra care and attention provided to his clean hands would improve his self satisfaction and also translates into cleaner workstations and better personal hygiene and appearance.

    ​

    • This collectively reflects in customer's mentality to keep the space cleaner and treat it with respect.

    Ideation

    • Synectics

    • Brainstorming

    Outcomes of Ideation

    • It was understood that a two-pronged approach would be necessary to bring about a behavioral change in the vendors. There is an overall driver which forms the basis of all communication and priming material, which would trigger their intrinsic motivation, and a product intervention would help them achieve the desired behavior of clean hands.

    Observations: usage & impact of intervention

    • Out of the 6 times, the street vendor served panipuri, he only wiped his hands with the given cloth 2 times. In both of these 2 times, the vendor looked at us standing there to observe him, so our presence served as a nudge for him to wipe his hands with the given cloth.

    • The timing of interacting with the street vendor was during his peak time of customer footfall, hence distraction.

    ​

    • 'clean' nature of the cloth deterred the vendor from making it dirty

    ​

    • Cloth was against the natural way the vendor wipes his hands,

    Addressing Behavior Change comes with multiple iterations on field

    Conclusion

    • The extensive study pointed at hygiene being a major factor in shaping perceptions around street food. It significantly contributes to the attitudes of customers towards street food vendors and their general behaviour in that space: the misuse of informal behaviour.

    • At this stage, the project concludes with an understanding that vendors agree that

    • Maintaining personal hygiene is necessary

    • Appearance plays a huge role when it comes to customers choosing to go to a thela/stall or not

    Learnings

    • Our intervention was focused on 3 parts:

    • 1. Product to induce professionalism

    • 2. Priming to create intrinsic motivation for vendors

    • 3. Poster to create expectation from customers.

    • Out of these, the product intervention was most easily adopted while the priming activity worked best in a narrative format, presented when the vendor was least occupied.

    Further Improvements

    • We have identified that to make a better impact, vendors of a community may need to be primed as a group. It will encourage discussions and further the intrinsic motivation.

    ​

    • The product intervention of wiping cloth needs to be made more distinguishable.

    ​

    • Habit of using the workstations cloth needs to be broken. Motivation for this needs to be identified.
